description: Coding skills required: HTML, CSS, Javascript, SQL, Python
summary:
ORBITAL 2.0 is a browser-based visual-novel game that teaches space mission design. The player takes the mission director’s chair, and the story calls them “user”. Mission 001, Asteroid Reconnaissance, targets NASA’s asteroid Bennu. The player makes three decisions, each a trade-off: mission approach, observation strategy and science payload, with a simplified 10-unit payload capacity. ORION, an AI assistant, states the objective and shows NASA data. A wrong choice fails the mission, the crew explains why, and the player retries that decision. A completed mission shows a design score and unlocks the next one.

It addresses the challenge by letting players experience integrated engineering decisions, with consequences and explained feedback, instead of studying isolated topics. The story-led format needs no prior knowledge.

It matters because learners rarely get to experiment with whole missions. ORBITAL 2.0 makes mission design approachable and shows why each choice affects the outcome. It is currently single-player; team play and richer resources are planned next.
details:
What it does and how it works

ORBITAL 2.0 is a story-driven mission design game that runs in a web browser. After a title screen and a transition video, the player opens a mission-select screen. Mission 001, Asteroid Reconnaissance, plays as a visual novel with typed dialogue, and Space advances each line. The player makes three decisions: mission approach, observation strategy and science payload. A wrong choice fails the mission with a stated reason, and the player retries only that decision. Clearing the mission shows a mission design score and an achievement, and unlocks the next mission.

Benefits

  • It needs no background in space science. Concepts are explained in plain words by the characters.
  • It shows why a decision matters, not just that it was wrong.
  • It uses real NASA facts about Bennu and OSIRIS-REx, such as its 492 m diameter and 4.3-hour rotation.
  • It runs with no install, and progress is saved on the device.

Intended impact

To make mission design approachable for students and curious beginners, and to show that every engineering choice is a trade-off. The game is built so that more missions can be added later.

Tools and technology

  • Code: HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript, with no framework. The story is kept in a data file, so new missions can be added without changing the game engine.
  • Browser features: Web Audio for small interface sounds, local storage for progress and settings, and the Gamepad API so a controller button works on the title screen.
  • Fonts: Orbitron and Rajdhani from Google Fonts.
  • Testing: automated Playwright runs in headless Chromium, which played Mission 001 from start to finish.
  • AI tools: Claude for the code, ChatGPT for image assets, and Gemini for character images.
  • Hardware: none beyond a normal computer.

Creativity

  • It turns engineering trade-offs into a narrative, with a crew, an AI assistant and a fictional agency.
  • The cyberpunk HUD interface has animated backgrounds.
  • Failure is a lesson: the player gets an explanation and an instant retry, with no replay of the chapter.
  • The two crew leads, the Engineer and the Scientist, represent the game’s two creators.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: NASA facts are labelled as real data. The 10-unit payload values are simplified game numbers, and the game says so on screen.
  • Scope: the Orbital Exploration Directorate and its characters are fictional.
  • Smoothness: assets are preloaded, and placeholders show if an image is missing.
  • Current limits: single-player, one playable mission, and one modelled resource. Team play and budget, power or mass management are future work.
  • Transparency: the AI tools used are credited.
